headline: Ohio Tourism Board Mandates Map Disarmament, Experts Call It a 'Scenic Disaster'
deck: In a bid to foster 'spontaneous adventures,' state officials decree mapmakers must now embrace oral traditions and trivial trivia.
article:
In a move that has left many scratching their heads, the Ohio Tourism Board has enacted an emergency measure mandating the disarmament of all mapmakers statewide. Citing the chaos of perpetual rediscovery, officials announced that aspiring mapmakers must now submit a 50-page application for a coveted 'Mapmaking License.' This convoluted process includes a psychological evaluation and a weekly pilgrimage to the nearest historical landmark, where applicants must answer Ohio trivia questions that only a true Buckeye could possibly fathom.

Tourism officials are convinced that the state must pivot to a navigation strategy they are calling 'Oral Tradition.' This initiative will give rise to 'Guided Rediscovery Tours,' where participants will unearth Ohio’s hidden attractions solely through storytelling. With aspirations of transforming the state into a cultural hotspot, locals are gearing up for a Massachusetts-like boom in folklore about such destinations as 'The Former Home of Some Guy Named Ted' and 'The Slightly Overhyped Midwestern Waterfall.'

Amid this bureaucratic whirlwind, confusion reigns in local towns as residents fervently debate the correct pronunciation of 'Cleveland.' This has led to a decade-long legal dispute over its official spelling, with current contenders including 'Cleavland,' 'Clevland,' and a proposed but controversial 'Clevand,' which some argue strikes a necessary poetic chord in Ohio’s literary landscape. Local resident Mabel Hargrove, who spends her evenings researching historical pronunciations, quipped, "Who needs maps when we have debates like these?"
author: Jasper D. Navigus, Senior Correspondent

oped.title: A Top Hat Tragedy: Why the Real Problem Lies in Ohio's Headgear
oped.author: Sir Ignatius Mapless, Chief Cartographer of the Imaginary
oped.body: Dear readers, as we gaze upon the Ohio Tourism Board's latest mandate to abandon maps in favor of oral traditions, one must ponder: is this not simply a thinly veiled attack on our beloved headwear? I argue that it is the hats—which, let’s face it, are in dire need of a fashion intervention—that are the true culprits behind this ‘scenic disaster.’ For too long, the floppy brims and garish feathers have distracted explorers from discovering the wonders of which Ohio so proudly boasts! Instead of maps, I propose we mandate all visitors wear only helmets—safety first, after all! In the end, mark my words, Ohio will flourish, not through spontaneous adventure but through a sartorial renaissance! So grab your helmets, ditch your maps, and let’s rediscover the lost art of headgear etiquette. Long live the uncharted Ohio!

stories.headline: Local GPS Company Files Bankruptcy as Map Disarmament Predicament Deepens
stories.deck: Their slogan now reads, 'Lost but not alone.'
stories.article:
In a twist of fate, Quantum Navigators, the leading GPS company in the region, has declared bankruptcy following Ohio's recent map disarmament. Once a tech titan, the firm struggled against rising customer complaints about being routed through 'mystical glades' and 'neighborhoods with lawn flamingo populations that could rival suburbia.'

Experts speculate that the only surviving segment of the business may be their quirky 'Lost and Found' hotline, which now offers frustrated callers the chance to buy a genuine wood-carved sign pointing to 'Somewhere in Ohio' for just $49.99.

stories.headline: New Play Explores Life in Ohio Through Verbal Directions, Leaves Audiences Utterly Confused
stories.deck: Critics applaud its complexity; audiences applaud the exit signs.
stories.article:
The avant-garde production 'Turn Left at the Raccoon Tree' has taken the Ohio theater scene by storm, but audience reactions have been a mixed bag. The play employs a series of elaborate oral directions to convey a complex narrative about lost socks and misplaced dreams, leaving viewers scratching their heads—or worse, wandering out into the parking lot in search of their cars.

While some critics hailed its innovation in dramatic storytelling, many felt the real drama lay in not knowing how to get home afterward, leading to an impromptu discussion group forming outside the theater revolving around various interpretations of 'cross the creek by the swing set.'

stories.headline: New Trend: Families Rediscovering Ancestors by Following Oral Directions to Ohio
stories.deck: It's like 'Roots,' but with more detours.
stories.article:
In an unexpected movement sweeping suburban America, families are hitting the road to reconnect with their Ohioan roots—all thanks to oral direction maps. Enthusiasts report a sense of kinship rarely felt in the digital age, albeit confused by the requirement to turn left at the 'old oak with the tire swing' and right after 'the place where they used to sell homemade pies.'

Local historians are rubbing their hands in delight, noting that as families wander through random cornfields and neighborhood yards, they inadvertently unearth previously unsung tales of suburban life, such as Grandma’s epic battle with a raccoon over the family barbecue sauce recipe.
